"Forthcoming" is one of those words that carries two quite different meanings depending on the context. Both meanings, however, share a hidden common thread: the idea of something coming forward — either toward you in time, or from inside a person outward into the open. Once you see that thread, the word becomes easy to remember.

It also has a third, related meaning that you'll come across in formal writing. All three are covered here.
Meaning 1: Coming Soon / About to Happen

This is the most straightforward meaning. When something is described as "forthcoming," it simply means it is planned, expected, and on its way in the near future — a more polished way of saying "upcoming" or "coming soon."

Her forthcoming novel has already attracted a lot of attention. (The novel hasn't been released yet, but it will be soon.)

The forthcoming election is expected to be extremely competitive.

Details of the forthcoming merger were kept confidential.

What this meaning implies that "upcoming" doesn't quite capture: A forthcoming thing is not merely a possibility — it is already confirmed and in the pipeline. If someone says "her forthcoming book," it means the book is definitely being published, not just being considered.

Where you'll spot this meaning: The word almost always sits directly before a noun — a forthcoming book, a forthcoming report, a forthcoming announcement, a forthcoming season. If you see "forthcoming" placed right before a person, place, or thing, this is the meaning in play.
Meaning 2: Willing to Share Information / Open and Communicative

This is where the word gets more interesting and more commonly misunderstood. When used to describe a person (or an organization), "forthcoming" means they are open, willing, and ready to share information — especially without needing to be pushed, pressured, or questioned repeatedly.

Picture two witnesses being interviewed after an incident. The first one gives full, clear, honest answers and even volunteers details that weren't asked about. The second gives vague, evasive replies and makes you drag every piece of information out of them. The first witness is forthcoming. The second is not.

The witness was very forthcoming during the investigation. (She shared information openly and cooperatively.)

He wasn't forthcoming about why he had left the company. (He was reluctant to share the real reasons.)

The government has become more forthcoming with the public about its data collection practices. (More transparent and open than it used to be.)

A very important nuance: This meaning is used in a negative or limited sense far more often than in a positive one. You will hear "not forthcoming," "less than forthcoming," and "hardly forthcoming" all the time. The reason is that when someone is fully open and sharing, we usually just say they were "honest" or "open" or "transparent." The word "forthcoming" tends to get deployed precisely when someone is falling short of that — when we're noting the absence or scarcity of openness. Keep an ear out for this pattern.

Where you'll spot this meaning: The word almost always comes after a verb, especially the verb "be" — was forthcoming, isn't forthcoming, has been forthcoming. And it almost always describes a person or an institution, not a physical thing or an event.
Meaning 3: Being Provided or Made Available

This is a slightly more formal and less common meaning, but you will encounter it — particularly in journalism, official writing, and British English.

Here, "forthcoming" describes whether something that was expected — usually help, money, support, an answer, or an apology — was actually provided or not.

The promised funding was not forthcoming. (The money was expected, but it never actually arrived or was given.)

An apology from the organization was not forthcoming. (No apology came, even though one was due.)

Support was forthcoming from several unexpected sources. (Help did come, from places no one anticipated.)

Notice that in this meaning, "not forthcoming" is very common. It's a formal way of saying something that was expected simply never materialized — it was withheld, delayed indefinitely, or never provided at all.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

You'll almost never be confused if you ask yourself these two questions:

Is the word describing a person/organization, or a thing/event? If a person or organization is being described as forthcoming (or not), it's Meaning 2 — their willingness to share information. If a thing is being described, it's either Meaning 1 (an event coming soon) or Meaning 3 (something being provided or not provided).

Where does the word sit in the sentence? When "forthcoming" comes before a noun — her forthcoming album, the forthcoming summit — it almost always means "coming soon" (Meaning 1). When it comes after a verb — she was forthcoming, help was not forthcoming — it's either Meaning 2 or Meaning 3.

Many people confuse these two words. They sound similar and are related in spirit, but they are genuinely different.

Forthright means being direct and blunt in how you say things. A forthright person gets straight to the point without dancing around it, sometimes at the expense of tact.

Forthcoming (in Meaning 2) means being willing to share information in the first place.

You can be forthcoming but not forthright — you share information freely, but you do so diplomatically and gently. You can be forthright but not forthcoming — you're direct and blunt about what you choose to share, but you're evasive about the things you'd rather keep quiet. The two words often overlap in practice, but they describe different qualities. "Forthcoming" is about willingness to open up. "Forthright" is about directness in delivery.

"Forthcoming" is a moderately formal word. You'll encounter it most in journalism, official statements, professional emails, academic writing, and legal or political contexts. It's not unusual in everyday speech either, but it carries a slightly elevated tone. A person writing casually might say "his next book" rather than "his forthcoming book," or "she didn't say much" rather than "she wasn't very forthcoming." When you use this word yourself, it will sound polished and precise.

As an adjective, "forthcoming" has three closely related meanings.

It can describe something that is coming soon and already planned — a forthcoming announcement, a forthcoming season, a forthcoming report. It can describe a person or organization that is willing to share information openly — being forthcoming about one's past, not being forthcoming with the press. And it can describe whether something expected was actually provided or made available — help was forthcoming; the support was not forthcoming.

The word is formal in tone, most often appears in negative constructions when used in the "sharing information" sense, and should never be confused with "forthright," which is about directness of manner rather than willingness to open up.
